End-of-chapter exercises are tightly scaffolded and single-task by design. Real data work isn't — students need open-ended prompts where they pick a question, do the analysis end-to-end, and communicate results. This page collects ten such prompts at three scales.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to use this bank"}
Pick prompts that match where students are in the term:

- **After Ch 3**: Mini #1 or #2 (visualization-only)
- **After Ch 7**: Mini #3 or #4, or any Mid prompt
- **After Ch 9**: Any Mid prompt
- **After Ch 11**: Any Capstone prompt

Pair every prompt with one or more rubrics from the [rubrics library](rubrics.html). The recommended rubric is listed under each prompt.
:::

| Scale | Time | Chapters needed | Prompts |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mini** | 1-2 weeks | Ch 1-3 (visualization) or Ch 1-5 (with regression) | #1-4 |
| **Mid** | 2-4 weeks | Ch 1-7 (with confidence intervals) | #5-7 |
| **Capstone** | 4+ weeks / semester | Ch 1-11 (full pipeline) | #8-10 |

---

# Mini-projects (1-2 weeks)

## #1 — *What's in this dataset?*

**Scale**: 1 week. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-3. **Skills**: data import, EDA, ggplot2, dplyr.

**The prompt**: You'll be given (or you'll choose) a real dataset of at least 500 rows and 6 variables. Your job is to **write a one-page profile of the dataset** for someone who has never seen it. The profile should answer: What is each variable? What does the data look like? What surprised you?

**Deliverables**:
- A `.qmd` that knits to a 1-page HTML report
- 3-5 well-labeled figures (no `ggplot()` defaults — titles, axis labels, captions)
- A "data dictionary" table: variable name, type, units, range, missing %
- 200-300 words of prose

**Dataset suggestions**:
- `palmerpenguins::penguins` — accessible, lots of variable types
- `nycflights13::flights` (sample of 10k rows) — bigger, more wrangling
- A student-chosen `tidytuesdayR` dataset from [tidytuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)

**Suggested rubric**: [Code quality](rubrics.html#code-quality) (50%) + [Written explanation](rubrics.html#written-explanation--report) (50%).

**Scaffold**:
- Day 1-2: import the data, run `glimpse()` + `skim()`, write the data dictionary
- Day 3-5: build the figures; iterate on one until it's actually informative
- Day 6-7: write prose; knit; submit

---

## #2 — *One question, one chart*

**Scale**: 1 week. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-3. **Skills**: focused EDA, ggplot2 polish.

**The prompt**: Pick ONE question you can answer with ONE chart from a dataset of your choice. Iterate on that chart until a non-statistician would understand it at a glance.

**Deliverables**:
- A single `.png` (300+ dpi, suitable for print) of the final chart
- A 100-word caption that states the question and the answer
- A "design diary" appendix: 3-5 earlier versions of the chart with notes on what you changed and why

**Dataset suggestions**:
- Any [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/data) CSV
- `gapminder::gapminder` for trend questions
- A local dataset (campus, city) for relevance

**Suggested rubric**: a single-criterion rubric: "Is the chart's answer clear at first glance to a non-statistician?" (Excellent / Proficient / Developing / Beginning). Optional second criterion: "Design-diary evidence of iteration."

**Why it works**: forces a discipline of polish that scaffolded exercises don't reward. Students who get 4s here tend to keep that polish in later work.

---

## #3 — *Compare two groups*

**Scale**: 2 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-5 (or 1-9 if hypothesis-testing required). **Skills**: EDA, dplyr `group_by()`, 2-sample comparison.

**The prompt**: Pick a numerical variable that varies across two groups in some dataset, and answer: **does the difference look real?** Use whatever tools the course has covered so far: side-by-side visualizations after Ch 3, summary statistics + boxplots after Ch 4, a fitted simple regression after Ch 5, or a formal hypothesis test after Ch 9.

**Deliverables**:
- A 2-3 page report (`.qmd` → HTML or PDF)
- At least one visualization comparing the groups
- A numerical comparison appropriate to the course content covered
- A 200-word "what I would do with more data / chapters" section

**Dataset suggestions**:
- `palmerpenguins::penguins` — flipper length by species
- `nycflights13::flights` — departure delay by carrier
- A dataset of student-collected data (a class survey, a campus measurement)

**Suggested rubric**: [Data analysis project](rubrics.html#data-analysis-project-mini-project) (full).

**Variants**:
- *No-hypothesis-test version* (after Ch 5): use confidence intervals + visualization only
- *Hypothesis-test version* (after Ch 9): use a formal test with assumptions checked

---

## #4 — *Regression debrief*

**Scale**: 2 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-6. **Skills**: simple/multiple regression, interpretation, EDA.

**The prompt**: Fit a regression model with one numerical outcome and 1-2 predictors on a dataset of your choice. Write a debrief explaining what the coefficients mean **in domain terms** (with units), what the R² tells you, and which conclusions you'd be careful about drawing.

**Deliverables**:
- A 2-page debrief that a domain expert (not a statistician) could read
- The fitted model summary (in an appendix)
- A residuals-vs-fitted plot with a one-paragraph interpretation
- Explicit discussion of causation vs. association

**Dataset suggestions**:
- `palmerpenguins::penguins` — body mass on flipper length + species
- `moderndive::evals` — teaching evaluation score on beauty + age (built-in)
- `gapminder` — life expectancy on GDP per capita + continent

**Suggested rubric**: [Data analysis project](rubrics.html#data-analysis-project-mini-project) — emphasize Interpretation row.

---

# Mid-scale projects (2-4 weeks)

## #5 — *Sampling investigation*

**Scale**: 3 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-7 (sampling). **Skills**: experimental design, sampling distributions, virtual sampling.

**The prompt**: Design a **virtual sampling experiment**. Pick a population (a dataset you'll treat as "the truth"), a statistic of interest (mean, median, proportion, regression slope), and study how the sampling distribution behaves as $n$ varies. Vary $n$ across at least 4 sample sizes and visualize the result.

**Deliverables**:
- A 3-4 page report
- A faceted figure showing the sampling distribution at each $n$
- A summary table: sample size, mean of $\hat{\theta}$, SD of $\hat{\theta}$
- A 250-word section: "What does the Central Limit Theorem predict here, and does it hold?"

**Dataset suggestions**:
- `moderndive::pennies_sample` (or any dataset with >10k rows that you can treat as a population)
- `nycflights13::flights$air_time` — sampling distribution of the mean
- A simulated population (uniform, exponential, bimodal) — lets you change the population shape

**Suggested rubric**: [Data analysis project](rubrics.html#data-analysis-project-mini-project), with extra weight on Method choice.

---

## #6 — *Inference for a real question*

**Scale**: 3 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-9. **Skills**: confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, assumption checking.

**The prompt**: Find a real claim ("women earn 80% of what men do", "this drug works", "this policy reduced crime by 12%") in the news or a journal. Get the relevant data (or a close proxy). Re-do the inference using the techniques from Ch 8-9. Report:

- What does YOUR confidence interval / test say?
- How does it compare to the original claim?
- What assumptions did your analysis make? Are they plausible?
- What would change your conclusion?

**Deliverables**:
- A 4-page report with explicit links to the original claim
- Confidence interval(s) and/or hypothesis test(s) appropriate to the question
- Assumption-check section (LINE / sampling)
- 300-word "limitations" section

**Dataset suggestions**:
- [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/) datasets (often downloadable)
- [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/data/) microdata
- [TidyTuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday) datasets paired with news stories

**Suggested rubric**: [Data analysis project](rubrics.html#data-analysis-project-mini-project) + [Ethics/responsible-use criterion from Capstone](rubrics.html#final-capstone-all-in-one).

---

## #7 — *Multiple regression for a stakeholder*

**Scale**: 3-4 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-10. **Skills**: multiple regression, model comparison, professional communication.

**The prompt**: A stakeholder (real or imagined: a campus department, a small business, a non-profit) has a decision to make and you have data that might inform it. Build a multiple regression that gives them a quantitative answer. The "stakeholder" is non-technical.

**Deliverables**:
- A 2-page **executive summary** for the stakeholder (no jargon)
- A 4-page **technical appendix** for a peer (full model, diagnostics, assumptions)
- One headline figure
- Explicit discussion of WHAT the model can and can't tell them

**Dataset suggestions**:
- Real campus data (registrar's office; advancement office; sustainability office often have data + questions)
- `moderndive::amazon_books` for a books-pricing model
- A small business' actual data (with permission)

**Suggested rubric**: [Data analysis project](rubrics.html#data-analysis-project-mini-project) + [Written explanation](rubrics.html#written-explanation--report) (for the exec summary).

**Why it works**: forces students to write two registers — technical and lay — for the same analysis. That skill is rare and valuable.

---

# Capstone projects (4+ weeks / semester)

## #8 — *End-to-end pipeline*

**Scale**: 4-6 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-11. **Skills**: every chapter; reproducibility.

**The prompt**: Pick a question YOU care about. Get the data (download, scrape with permission, or use an API). Wrangle it, explore it, model it, communicate it. Submit a reproducible repo that anyone can run.

**Deliverables**:
- A public Git repo with: README, scripts (numbered), data (or download script), final report (`.qmd` → HTML)
- A 5-7 page report following Ch 11's "tell your story" structure
- At least one figure, one model, one summary table
- A `setup.R` that installs every package used, so a grader can run the code on a clean machine

**Dataset constraints** (to keep scope honest):
- Must be REAL (not simulated)
- At least 1,000 rows
- At least one numerical AND one categorical variable
- Has to come from a documented source you can cite

**Suggested rubric**: [Final capstone](rubrics.html#final-capstone-all-in-one) (full).

**Scaffold (checkpoints)**:
- Week 1: question + data source proposal (instructor approves)
- Week 2: data acquired + EDA in repo
- Week 3: at least one model fit; preliminary results in repo
- Week 4-5: write report; iterate
- Week 6: final submit + present

---

## #9 — *Replication / extension study*

**Scale**: 5-8 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-11 + reading academic papers. **Skills**: scientific replication, methodological critique.

**The prompt**: Find a published paper (peer-reviewed or working paper) that has public data. **Replicate** one of its main findings using the data and the methods covered in this course. Then **extend**: either critique a methodological choice and re-do the analysis, or add a robustness check the original didn't include.

**Deliverables**:
- A 6-8 page report:
  - Section 1: paper + original finding
  - Section 2: your replication (with code)
  - Section 3: agreement / disagreement with the original
  - Section 4: your extension and what it changes
- A repo (same standards as #8)
- A 1-page "what I learned about science" reflection

**Paper suggestions** (point students to):
- [American Economic Association](https://www.aeaweb.org/journals) replication-policy journals
- [Reproducibility in Cancer Biology](https://elifesciences.org/collections/9b1e83d1/reproducibility-project-cancer-biology) datasets
- [Open Science Framework](https://osf.io/) registered reports

**Suggested rubric**: [Final capstone](rubrics.html#final-capstone-all-in-one) (full) + [Peer code review](rubrics.html#peer-code-review) framing for the critique section.

**Why it works**: students learn that "the literature" is not infallible, and they get hands-on experience with what reproducibility means. Highest-impact prompt for students considering grad school.

---

## #10 — *Build something useful for someone*

**Scale**: 6-12 weeks. **Prereqs**: Ch 1-11 + project management. **Skills**: scoping, stakeholder management, end-to-end delivery.

**The prompt**: Find a client (a campus office, a non-profit, a class friend, a community group) with a data question. Scope the work with them. Deliver something they will actually use. The "deliverable" might be: a Shiny dashboard, a recurring report, a recommendation memo, a cleaned dataset, a process improvement.

**Deliverables**:
- A 2-page scoping memo signed off by the client (week 2)
- The delivered artifact (whatever it is — must be runnable / usable, not just a `.qmd`)
- A 4-page reflection: what you scoped, what you actually delivered, what changed, what you'd do differently
- Client sign-off email confirming the deliverable was useful

**Suggested rubric**: [Final capstone](rubrics.html#final-capstone-all-in-one) + [Group collaboration](rubrics.html#group-collaboration) (if team-based).

**Setup tips for instructors**:
- Find clients **before** the term starts. Campus admin offices, libraries, sustainability, advancement, athletics often have backlogs.
- Have a back-up plan for clients who flake. Pre-vet a list of "always-available" projects (e.g., from the library or your own research).
- Reserve veto on scope — students will over-promise. Lock scope at week 2 with the client present.

**Why it works**: this is the closest thing to actual professional data work students will do before they graduate. Connections from this prompt frequently turn into internships or jobs.

---

## Choosing prompts for your course

**One-and-done courses** (intro stats, no capstone tradition): use one Mini prompt (#1, #2, or #4) as a 1-2 week mid-semester project. Boosts engagement; doesn't blow up the syllabus.

**Two-semester sequences**: a Mini in semester 1, a Mid in semester 2. Or a Mini early in semester 1, a Capstone in semester 2.

**Stats-for-majors capstone courses**: use #8 or #9 as the spine of the course; supplement with the [TA guide](ta-guide.html) for managing milestones.

**Community-engaged / project-based courses**: #10 is built for you. Allow a full term for scoping + delivery.

::: {.callout-note title="Workload calibration"}
Rough effort estimates per student-hour, assuming average preparation:

| Scale | Hours of student work | Hours of instructor grading |
|---|---|---|
| Mini | 5-10 | 0.5 per student |
| Mid | 15-25 | 1-2 per student |
| Capstone | 40-80 | 2-4 per student + advising |

Add roughly 30% if students are pre-Ch 7 (they're still learning the tools).
:::
